PAPER: JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Geng et al Original Paper Predictors of Professional Responses in Nonprofit Mental Health Forums: Interpretable Machine Learning Analysis Shuang Geng1, DPhil; Yanghui Li2, MEng; Jie Wang2, MEng; Peixuan Chen3, MSci; Xusheng Wu4, MEng; Zhiqun Zhang5, MSci 1College of Management, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China 2College of Artificial Intelligence, Shenzhen University, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China 3School of Life Sciences, Central South University, Changsha, Hunan, China 4Shenzhen Health Development Research and Data Management Center, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China 5Shenzhen Traditional Chinese Medicine Hospital, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China Corresponding Author: Xusheng Wu, MEng Shenzhen Health Development Research and Data Management Center 5 Yuanling Road, Futian Shenzhen, Guangdong, 518000 China Phone: 86 19928750177 Email: jysgwuxusheng@163.com Abstract Background: Online mental health communities increase access and equity for patients seeking psychological support. User demand and professional contributions are key to their sustainability. While previous research has examined factors influencing physicians’participation in online consultation platforms, limited attention has been given to how post characteristics affect the quantity and length of professional responses in nonprofit mental health communities. Objective: This study aims to examine how textual (ie, topic, sentiment, title length, and content length) and contextual (ie, page views and posting time) characteristics of inquiries in nonprofit mental health forums influence the quantity and length of responses from mental health professionals, providing insights for enhancing community interactions. Methods: We collected 18,572 question-and-answer records from a Chinese online mental health platform (August 2024-July 2025). Topic features were extracted using BERTopic, and sentiment features were obtained through a distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers–based sentiment classification model. Additional features were derived from post metadata. We compared 5 machine learning models and identified Light Gradient Boosting Machine as the best performer. We then applied Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis to it to evaluate the feature contributions to the prediction of response quantity and length. Results: In virtual mental health communities, user inquiries fall into 7 topic categories: work, love, depression, boyfriends or girlfriends, school, marriage, and family. Depression-related topics negatively predict response quantity, whereas interpersonal, school, marriage, or family topics are positively correlated. SHAP analysis revealed that page views (SHAP value=0.187) and title length (SHAP value=0.073) are key factors in predicting response quantity, and content length (SHAP value=0.274), sentiment category (SHAP value=0.054), and title length (SHAP value=0.053) are key factors in predicting response length. Posts exhibiting negative emotions are positively related to both the predicted quantity and length of responses, and this effect becomes more pronounced as the degree of emotional intensity increases. Titles with 15-20 characters and content with more than 60 characters are positively correlated with responses, whereas titles with fewer than 7 characters have negative effects. Higher view counts and weekday posts also increase response likelihood. Conclusions: This study provides insights into how textual and contextual features of patient posts influence professional responses in nonprofit mental health forums. It enhances understanding of voluntary knowledge contribution behaviors in online mental health communities and offers practical guidance for optimizing platform functional design and user posting strategies. JSON: Name: omhc_response_predictors_interpretable_ml Title: Interpretable gradient-boosting analysis of post-level textual and contextual predictors of professional reply quantity and length in nonprofit online mental health forums Short Hypothesis: In nonprofit online mental health forums, posts with higher page views, stronger negative sentiment intensity, and longer content causally produce a greater number of and longer professional replies than posts with lower page views, weaker/positive sentiment, and shorter content. Related Work: Prior research on online mental health communities has analyzed user engagement, professional contribution, and community dynamics using regression, structural equation models, and some machine learning classifiers. Topic modeling and sentiment analysis have been applied to characterize post content and emotion, while a subset of studies has used tree-based ensembles and SVM/XGBoost models for prediction tasks. Existing approaches focus primarily on static user or professional attributes, binary response occurrence, or coarse measures of engagement rather than on continuous outcomes such as reply quantity and reply length. Limitations include limited interpretability of ensemble models, narrow feature sets (often excluding fine-grained textual signals like topic clusters and sentiment intensity), single-platform studies that reduce generalizability, and a lack of rigorous ablation and cross-platform robustness analyses. Causal claims are generally unsupported because of observational designs and insufficient control for confounders. Abstract: This project develops and evaluates an interpretable machine learning pipeline to identify post-level textual and contextual predictors of professional reply quantity and reply length in nonprofit online mental health forums. The pipeline integrates transformer-based sentiment scoring, density-aware topic clustering, engineered metadata features, and a gradient-boosting regression model with Shapley-based explanations to produce both accurate predictions and feature-level interpretability. The main contribution is a validated, reproducible pipeline that quantifies the effect sizes and nonlinear thresholds of topics, sentiment polarity and intensity, title/content length, page views, and posting time on two continuous outcomes: number of professional replies and average reply length. Expected outcomes include (1) a ranked set of actionable post-level predictors with interpretable effect directions and thresholds, (2) ablation evidence of feature-group importance, and (3) cross-platform robustness results that indicate limits of generalization. The deliverable is an open research pipeline for forum design and follow-up causal studies. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset = YiDianLing public Q&A posts (Aug 2024–Jul 2025), n≈18,572 raw; cleaned dataset n≈11,154 after topic-noise removal; robustness dataset = YiXinLi public forum (Dec 2024–Jul 2025). Preprocessing: remove empty-title/content posts; BERTopic clustering to extract topic id; DistilBERT-based sentence-level sentiment → aggregate polarity (negative/neutral/positive) and continuous intensity; log-transform length and view counts; encode temporal features. Prediction tasks: (A) regression target = log(reply_count + 1); (B) regression target = log(mean_reply_length). Baselines: ridge regression, linear regression with polynomial terms, SVM regression, random forest, XGBoost. Primary model: LightGBM with hyperparameter grid search. Metrics: MAE, MSE, R^2 for predictive accuracy; calibration plots; stability metrics = mean absolute SHAP value variance across 5 repeated random splits; statistical tests = paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test for MAE differences. Cross-validation: repeated 5×(70/30) random splits; report mean and SD. Ablations: (1) remove sentiment features; (2) remove topic features; (3) remove metadata features (page views, time); (4) use only title+content lengths; report delta MAE/MSE/R^2 per ablation. Robustness: train on YiDianLing, test on YiXinLi (out-of-platform generalization); retrain on YiXinLi and compare SHAP-ranked features. Additional checks: permutation importance, partial dependence plots for top 6 features, and sensitivity to BERTopic cluster threshold (compare cluster noise removal vs. keeping noise). Risk Factors and Limitations: Observational confounding: unobserved user and consultant attributes (diagnoses, consultant workload, reputation) may bias associations and preclude causal inference. Label noise: automated sentiment and topic models can misclassify emotion polarity/intensity and topic membership, producing biased feature estimates. Platform bias and generalizability: models trained on Chinese nonprofit forums may not transfer to other cultures, languages, or commercial platforms. Outcome validity: reply quantity and length are imperfect proxies for response quality and clinical usefulness. Data sparsity and imbalance: low-frequency topics or rare high-intensity sentiment posts may yield unstable SHAP estimates. Temporal nonstationarity: changes in platform policy or seasonal effects can alter predictive relationships. Model overfitting: high-cardinality categorical temporal features and engineered interactions risk overfitting without sufficient regularization. Privacy and reproducibility constraints: platform access and scraping restrictions may limit dataset sharing and independent replication. Compute constraints: transformer-based sentiment inference and repeated cross-validation increase compute needs, which may limit large-scale extensions or multimodal experiments.
